screens.title: Testing Smart Contracts and DApps
screens.narratorSegment: Testing smart contracts and DApps is not optional. Because deployed contracts are immutable and often hold value, a single bug can cause irreversible loss. In this chapter you will learn how to write thorough unit tests, run integration tests that exercise multi-contract interactions and frontend flows, measure gas consumption to find optimizations, and apply Test-Driven Development to guide secure design. We will use the established tooling for EVM chains, with a focus on Hardhat and its testing stack. You will see concrete examples, starting from a simple counter contract and moving to a token testing activity. Along the way we’ll show common pitfalls, such as relying only on happy-path tests or forgetting to reset blockchain state between tests. By the end you will understand how tests serve as safety nets, documentation, and performance checks for smart contract projects. Consider one question as you begin: what would a small, visible bug cost if your contract were live today? That perspective should guide the rigor of your tests.

screens.title: Why testing is critical for smart contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Testing for smart contracts is critical because once code is deployed on-chain, it cannot be changed without another transaction and often a migration. This immutability means that any logic error, missing access check, or unhandled edge case can be irreversible and costly. Begin by understanding testing as three complementary protections: unit tests validate individual functions and invariants, integration tests confirm that components work together, and gas analysis ensures the contract is efficient and economically viable. A concrete example: a missing require check in a withdraw function might allow unauthorized withdrawals. A unit test that attempts an unauthorized withdraw and expects a revert will catch this before deployment. A common misconception is that testing on a testnet is enough; while testnets are useful, local test suites provide deterministic, repeatable checks and faster iteration. Key takeaway: treat tests as design artifacts and documentation that prove correctness and inform safe upgrades. Ask yourself after each change: which tests would fail if this change introduced a regression? Why testing is critical for smart contracts means tests both document intended behavior and stop dangerous regressions before code reaches an immutable ledger.. In practical terms, immutable code demands exhaustive verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Testing Importance
Definition

Testing verifies contract correctness before deployment to an immutable environment. It reduces risk by catching logic and access-control bugs early.

Concrete example
A withdraw function missing an authorization check can be proven dangerous by a test that calls withdraw from an unauthorized account and expects a revert.
Common misconception
Relying only on manual testing or testnet deployment is insufficient. Automated suites give deterministic coverage and fast feedback.
Key Takeaway

Make tests part of design. If a change has no tests, ask why and add them before merging.

How tests protect value
  • Catch logic errors and miscalculations that could lock funds or drain balances.
  • Verify role-based access and prevent unauthorized operations.
  • Document expected behaviors through passing tests that also act as examples.
Try this
Write a unit test that asserts a critical function reverts when called by an unauthorized signer. If it passes, you cement a safety check that prevents a common exploit.

screens.title: Unit testing with Hardhat — Counter example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete unit test pattern using the Counter contract. The goal of unit testing is to isolate a single contract and verify each function under varied inputs. In Hardhat tests you'll commonly use a beforeEach hook to deploy a fresh contract instance and capture signers to simulate different users. For assertions, use Chai's expect functions to check return values, state variables, event emissions, and reverted transactions. A typical test set includes: start state verification; successful function behavior like increment; failing behavior, such as preventing decrement below zero; and gas tracking to measure operation cost. For example, increment should change count from zero to one and a test asserts that getCount equals one. To test a revert, call decrement on zero and use the revertedWith assertion to ensure the error message matches. A common mistake is sharing a deployed instance across tests, which creates brittle inter-test dependencies. Always deploy fresh instances in beforeEach to guarantee isolation. Final takeaway: unit tests are fast feedback loops that validate each function and its invariants before moving to wider integration tests. Unit testing with Hardhat — Counter example means deploy fresh instances per test, assert successful and failing cases, and track gas when relevant.. In practical terms, structure, assertions, and gas checks using mocha and chai. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Counter Unit Test
Test structure
Use beforeEach to deploy a fresh contract and get signers. Write separate it blocks for start state, success paths, failures, and gas checks.
// test/Counter.js\nconst { expect } = require("chai");\nconst { ethers } = require("hardhat");\n\ndescribe("Counter", function () {\n beforeEach(async function () {\n [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();\n const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");\n counter = await Counter.deploy();\n await counter.waitForDeployment();\n });\n\n it("starts at zero", async function () {\n expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);\n });\n});
Key assertions
  • expect(...).to.equal(...) for state values.
  • expect(...).to.be.revertedWith(...) for specific revert reasons.
  • Check events using to.emit(contract, "EventName").withArgs(...).
Gas check
Retrieve receipt.gasUsed after tx.wait() and log or assert upper bounds to detect costly operations early.
Key Takeaway

Unit tests should be isolated, fast, and include both success and failure checks plus occasional gas assertions.

screens.title: Unit Tests vs Integration Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Unit tests and integration tests serve different but complementary purposes. Unit tests examine one contract in isolation, proving function correctness and edge-case handling. They are fast, deterministic, and ideal for TDD. Integration tests exercise the interactions between multiple contracts or between contracts and the frontend, confirming that composed behaviors satisfy system-level requirements. For example, unit tests verify that a transfer updates balances correctly in a token contract. An integration test would deploy both token and staking contracts, perform a stake operation, and assert that tokens moved from the user to the staking contract and that staking state updated. A common misunderstanding is treating integration tests as a replacement for unit tests. They are slower and more complex; they do not replace the need for many focused unit tests. Integration tests are essential for orchestration bugs, race conditions, or incorrect message flows between contracts or with oracles. The closing insight: build a layered test suite — many fast unit tests for logic correctness and a smaller set of integration tests that validate interactions and real-world sequences. Unit Tests vs Integration Tests means use many isolated unit tests for logic, and targeted integration tests to validate interactions and end-to-end behavior.. In practical terms, when to isolate and when to exercise full flows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Unit vs Integration
Unit Tests
Isolate a single contract. Fast, many tests, used for TDD and edge-case verification.
  • Deploy fresh instance per test.
  • Assert state, events, and revert reasons.
  • Focus on single-function responsibilities.
Integration Tests
Deploy multiple contracts or connect frontend tools to a local chain to validate real flows and cross-contract invariants.
  • Test across contracts, oracles, and frontend interactions.
  • Slower but necessary for orchestration issues.
  • Often use a local network like Hardhat Network for deterministic behavior.
Concrete scenario
Unit test: ensure a token.transfer reduces sender balance. Integration test: transfer then stake in a staking contract, and assert final balances in both token and staking contracts plus emitted events.

screens.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) for smart contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Test-Driven Development is a cycle you can apply to smart contract work. The loop is simple: write a failing test that expresses the desired behavior, implement the minimal contract code to make the test pass, then refactor while keeping tests green. For smart contracts, TDD helps you think through edge conditions and access control before writing logic that could be hard to change later. Start with a small behavior, for example, a test that expects increment to raise the count. Run the test to see it fail. Implement increment in the contract, deploy in beforeEach, and run tests until they pass. After passing, refactor for readability or gas efficiency, then run tests again. A typical pitfall is writing overly broad tests that mask the precise failing condition. Prefer fine-grained tests that specify one behavior per test. TDD also makes it easier to add regression suites: as you add features, convert previously failing edge cases into automated checks. The key idea is that tests drive design choices and keep the contract safe as it evolves. Test-Driven Development (TDD) for smart contracts means writing the test first clarifies desired behavior and creates a regression net that supports safe refactoring.. In practical terms, a step-by-step tdd loop adapted for solidity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

1
Write a failing test
Express the expected behavior as a test. Keep it focused so failure points are clear.
2
Implement minimal code
Write just enough contract logic to satisfy the test, avoiding premature optimization.

screens.title: Measuring and analyzing gas costs
screens.narratorSegment: Measuring gas costs during testing is essential to produce efficient smart contracts. Every transaction returns a receipt containing gasUsed; capture and log it to understand how changes affect cost. For example, call increment and then await the transaction receipt, then inspect receipt. gasUsed to get a numeric cost. That raw number helps you compare implementations. Tools like hardhat-gas-reporter integrate into your test runs to produce per-function summaries, allowing you to spot gas-hungry functions across the suite. A practical example: replacing a loop with a mapping-based lookup often reduces gas significantly; you can validate this by comparing gasUsed before and after the refactor. A common misconception is to optimize prematurely: first write correct, well-tested code, then use gas measurements to focus on hotspots. Finally, use gas thresholds in tests when reasonable to detect regressions, but avoid brittle hard caps; instead, monitor trends and set actionable alerts. The core takeaway: measure before optimizing and use reporters for objective decisions. Measuring and analyzing gas costs means capture gasused per transaction and use reporting tools to find hotspots; optimize where tests show meaningful gains.. In practical terms, capture gasused and use reporters to optimize expensive operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Gas Analysis
Capture gasUsed
After sending a transaction, await tx.wait() and inspect receipt.gasUsed. Store or log values for comparison across commits.
// example\nconst tx = await contract.increment();\nconst receipt = await tx.wait();\nconsole.log(`Gas used: ${receipt.gasUsed.toString()}`);
Reporter
Use hardhat-gas-reporter to generate per-test gas metrics and compare functions across the test suite. This helps prioritize optimizations.
Optimization tip
Refactor hotspots verified by gas reports. Avoid optimizing code paths rarely used; focus on frequently called functions.

screens.title: Integration testing with DApp frontends
screens.narratorSegment: Integration tests that include the frontend validate the end-to-end experience users see. To achieve this, run a local blockchain like Hardhat Network and deploy your contracts there during the test setup. Use browser automation tools like Playwright or Cypress to simulate user actions: connect a test wallet, trigger transactions, and assert UI updates that depend on contract events. For example, a mint action in the frontend should call the contract, wait for the transaction, and then update the UI to show the new token. In your integration test, assert that the expected event was emitted by the contract and that the frontend shows the updated state. Mocks are helpful: if your frontend relies on an oracle, mock the oracle response so the test stays deterministic. A common pitfall is flakiness due to network timing; ensure tests wait for transaction confirmations and prefer faster local networks rather than unpredictable public testnets for CI. The core benefit is confidence that on-chain logic and user experience align under realistic conditions. Integration testing with DApp frontends means include frontend tests that exercise contract calls and event-driven ui changes against a local, deterministic chain to validate real user flows.. In practical terms, simulate user interactions with playwright or cypress against a local chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Integration + Frontend
Process
  1. Start a local chain and deploy contracts in test setup.
  2. Run a headless browser to load frontend connected to the local chain.
  3. Simulate wallet actions, send transactions, and wait for confirmations.
  4. Assert both on-chain state changes and frontend UI updates driven by events.

screens.title: Common testing pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring pitfalls when testing smart contracts that can create a false sense of security. The first is insufficient coverage: only testing happy paths misses unauthorized calls, boundary values, and unusual sequences. Ensure you include negative and edge-case tests. Second, shared state across tests causes unpredictable results; always deploy fresh contract instances in beforeEach or use snapshots to reset chain state. Third, neglecting access control tests lets privilege escalations slip through. Write tests that call privileged functions from unauthorized accounts and assert reverts with the correct messages. Fourth, not mocking external dependencies results in flaky tests; replace oracles and third-party contracts with deterministic mocks in your test environment. Fifth, hardcoding gas thresholds can create brittle tests when the compiler or optimization settings change; instead use trends and alerts. A practical mitigation strategy is to maintain a test checklist that covers positive, negative, and edge cases, and to require a minimum coverage percentage before merging. Remember: tests are only valuable if they are reliable, focused, and maintained along with the code. Common testing pitfalls and how to avoid them means design tests to be isolated, include negative cases, mock externals, and prefer stable assertions over brittle thresholds.. In practical terms, coverage gaps, shared state, and insufficient negative tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Activity: Write unit tests for MyToken
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement unit tests for a simple ERC-like token contract. Start by setting up a Hardhat project and placing the provided MyToken contract in the contracts directory. In your test file create signers for deployer and other accounts, deploy MyToken with an initial supply, and assert the deployer received the full supply. Next write a transfer test: transfer tokens from deployer to a receiver and assert balances update and Transfer events are emitted. Then test failing transfers by attempting to move more tokens than available and assert a revert with the correct message. For approvals, call approve from the owner and assert allowance updated, and then test transferFrom by having the approved spender move tokens on behalf of the owner. A useful pattern is to keep each assertion focused in its own it block and to deploy fresh state in beforeEach. A common mistake is not asserting event arguments; include checks for Transfer and Approval events where applicable. After writing tests, run npx hardhat test to validate. If all pass, you have a verified competency milestone demonstrating core token behaviors.

screens.title: Testing environment and safety rules
screens.narratorSegment: Keep testing environments safe and deterministic. Use a local development network such as Hardhat Network for rapid iteration and deterministic behavior. Never store or use real private keys in test or CI environments; use generated test accounts and ephemeral keys. For scenarios requiring external services, mock or stub oracles and third-party contracts so tests remain under your control. When moving to testnets, ensure you still run the full test suite locally first; testnets are useful for integration checks but are slower and less reliable for quick feedback. Another safety rule: avoid deploying to mainnet during development and testing. If a mainnet-like run is required, use a forked mainnet local node and run tests against a forked state with read-only checks, but keep any real keys out of CI. Always log gas usage on local runs and capture test reports in CI so regressions are visible. These practices reduce both security and operational risk when validating smart contracts and DApps. screens.title: Test lifecycle: from TDD to CI
screens.narratorSegment: A robust test lifecycle ensures tests remain useful as the codebase grows. Start locally with TDD: write failing tests, implement code, and iterate until they pass. Next, add unit tests into your repository so reviewers can see behavioral expectations. Configure CI to run the full test suite and gas reporter on each pull request to detect regressions early. When integrating frontend tests, run headless browser suites against a local chain in CI, or run them in a separate job to control resource needs. Maintain a coverage target and require a passing test run before merging. Periodically run a suite of integration smoke tests on a forked mainnet or a staging testnet to surface environment-specific issues while still avoiding real keys. Finally, when upgrading deployed contracts, run regression tests against a forked state to validate migration scripts. A common mistake is letting tests drift stale; keep tests in sync with refactors by updating or rewriting brittle assertions. The final takeaway: automation keeps your safety net effective and enforces consistent quality across teams. fullNarratorScript:
Testing smart contracts and DApps is not optional. Because deployed contracts are immutable and often hold value, a single bug can cause irreversible loss. In this chapter you will learn how to write thorough unit tests, run integration tests that exercise multi-contract interactions and frontend flows, measure gas consumption to find optimizations, and apply Test-Driven Development to guide secure design. We will use the established tooling for EVM chains, with a focus on Hardhat and its testing stack. You will see concrete examples, starting from a simple counter contract and moving to a token testing activity. Along the way we’ll show common pitfalls, such as relying only on happy-path tests or forgetting to reset blockchain state between tests. By the end you will understand how tests serve as safety nets, documentation, and performance checks for smart contract projects. Consider one question as you begin: what would a small, visible bug cost if your contract were live today? That perspective should guide the rigor of your tests.

These objectives focus your practice so you develop safe, testable smart contracts. First, you will write comprehensive unit tests using a framework like Hardhat or Truffle. That means deploying clean instances for each test, asserting state changes, and checking event emissions. Second, you will run integration tests that simulate contract-to-contract flows and frontend interactions, ensuring the whole system behaves as expected. Third, you will analyze gas usage during tests to find expensive operations and guide optimizations. Fourth, you will apply Test-Driven Development: write tests first, watch them fail, implement minimal code to pass, then refactor. Each objective has hands-on steps and a competency milestone so you can verify progress. For example, a milestone could be: a token contract with full unit tests that assert transfers, approvals, and event logs. Keep a testing mindset: tests are documentation, safety checks, and performance tools, not optional chores.

In addition to writing tests and measuring gas, you will learn to design test suites that catch common pitfalls. This includes testing negative and edge cases, verifying access control and event emission, and ensuring test isolation by resetting the chain state between tests. You will also learn to mock external dependencies such as oracles so integration tests remain deterministic. For a concrete example, when testing a staking flow, write a test that attempts unstaking with no balance and assert the revert reason. Finally, you will practice writing a test plan for a simple ERC-like token contract, covering deployment, transfers, approvals, and transferFrom behaviors. These practices increase confidence before any deployment to testnet or mainnet and reduce the likelihood of expensive mistakes. Learning Objectives — Continued means test negative and edge cases, mock external services, and reset state between tests to avoid flaky or misleading results.. In practical terms, skills to avoid common testing pitfalls and ensure robust coverage. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing for smart contracts is critical because once code is deployed on-chain, it cannot be changed without another transaction and often a migration. This immutability means that any logic error, missing access check, or unhandled edge case can be irreversible and costly. Begin by understanding testing as three complementary protections: unit tests validate individual functions and invariants, integration tests confirm that components work together, and gas analysis ensures the contract is efficient and economically viable. A concrete example: a missing require check in a withdraw function might allow unauthorized withdrawals. A unit test that attempts an unauthorized withdraw and expects a revert will catch this before deployment. A common misconception is that testing on a testnet is enough; while testnets are useful, local test suites provide deterministic, repeatable checks and faster iteration. Key takeaway: treat tests as design artifacts and documentation that prove correctness and inform safe upgrades. Ask yourself after each change: which tests would fail if this change introduced a regression? Why testing is critical for smart contracts means tests both document intended behavior and stop dangerous regressions before code reaches an immutable ledger.. In practical terms, immutable code demands exhaustive verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete unit test pattern using the Counter contract. The goal of unit testing is to isolate a single contract and verify each function under varied inputs. In Hardhat tests you'll commonly use a beforeEach hook to deploy a fresh contract instance and capture signers to simulate different users. For assertions, use Chai's expect functions to check return values, state variables, event emissions, and reverted transactions. A typical test set includes: start state verification; successful function behavior like increment; failing behavior, such as preventing decrement below zero; and gas tracking to measure operation cost. For example, increment should change count from zero to one and a test asserts that getCount equals one. To test a revert, call decrement on zero and use the revertedWith assertion to ensure the error message matches. A common mistake is sharing a deployed instance across tests, which creates brittle inter-test dependencies. Always deploy fresh instances in beforeEach to guarantee isolation. Final takeaway: unit tests are fast feedback loops that validate each function and its invariants before moving to wider integration tests. Unit testing with Hardhat — Counter example means deploy fresh instances per test, assert successful and failing cases, and track gas when relevant.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unit tests and integration tests serve different but complementary purposes. Unit tests examine one contract in isolation, proving function correctness and edge-case handling. They are fast, deterministic, and ideal for TDD. Integration tests exercise the interactions between multiple contracts or between contracts and the frontend, confirming that composed behaviors satisfy system-level requirements. For example, unit tests verify that a transfer updates balances correctly in a token contract. An integration test would deploy both token and staking contracts, perform a stake operation, and assert that tokens moved from the user to the staking contract and that staking state updated. A common misunderstanding is treating integration tests as a replacement for unit tests. They are slower and more complex; they do not replace the need for many focused unit tests. Integration tests are essential for orchestration bugs, race conditions, or incorrect message flows between contracts or with oracles. Test-Driven Development is a cycle you can apply to smart contract work. The loop is simple: write a failing test that expresses the desired behavior, implement the minimal contract code to make the test pass, then refactor while keeping tests green. For smart contracts, TDD helps you think through edge conditions and access control before writing logic that could be hard to change later. Start with a small behavior, for example, a test that expects increment to raise the count. Run the test to see it fail. Implement increment in the contract, deploy in beforeEach, and run tests until they pass. After passing, refactor for readability or gas efficiency, then run tests again. TDD also makes it easier to add regression suites: as you add features, convert previously failing edge cases into automated checks. The key idea is that tests drive design choices and keep the contract safe as it evolves.
